hits.text:
Anthropic went after the largest bacterium ever found, a single cell you can see with the naked eye, and read the machinery packed inside it.

The size was never the interesting part. The question was how one cell keeps millions of copies of its own factory working in sync.

> COUNT - every ribosome location in the cell mapped, rather than averaged across it
> WRAP - the membrane sacs holding DNA and ribosomes treated as separate rooms
> FLOW - what each room produces compared against what sits next to it
> SPLIT - rooms with different output flagged as independent units
> SCALE - the whole layout tested against how large a normal cell can grow

Bacteria are supposed to be simple bags. One compartment, everything mixed, nothing filed away.

This one files. Its DNA and its ribosomes sit inside membranes, which textbooks reserve for complex cells.

That single arrangement is what lifts the size ceiling. A cell without rooms hits a physical wall long before a centimetre.

The rooms are not identical either. Output varies from one to the next, meaning parts of the same cell are doing different jobs.

That edges close to what tissue does, inside something that is still one organism by every definition we use.

The line between simple and complex life was drawn before anyone had seen this, and it was drawn on compartments.

Every room, its output and the size math behind it sit in the breakdown below.

holy sh*t . Jev Founder, Diogo Almeida just released a 11-page PDF whole Jev + AI agents loop

this is a 9-step blueprint on how to run your LLM through agents without paying frontier prices for every fork they hit:

step 1 → split the loop into three kinds of work: generation stays with the LLM, exact rules like action and spend caps stay in code, every fork in between becomes a typed question to Jev

step 2 → start every job with one Noul: is this in scope, or does it need a human before anything runs

step 3 → dispatch with a Choice: research, write or review. act only at confidence 0.85+, everything below goes to review

step 4 → call the LLM only where text has to be written: planning the task and filling tool arguments, nothing else

step 5 → gate every tool call before it runs: allow, confirm or block, plus a destructive check in the same round trip

step 6 → score what comes back: drop, summary or keep. nothing gets rewritten, so nothing is lost to a bad paraphrase

step 7 → close with two checks: Jev says the goal is met above 0.8, then code proves the file actually exists

step 8 → send the risky tail to a human: irreversible, touches money or visible outside the company gets a person whatever the confidence

step 9 → move one fork first and track three numbers for a week: cost per completed task, time per completed task, how often escalation fired and whether it was right

hits.name: Gipp
hits.text:
jev + opus 5.5 is one of those setups that makes agent architecture feel weirdly overcomplicated in hindsight.

the useful split isn’t “small model vs big model.” it’s deciding which calls actually need generation at all.

→ jev routes the next worker  
→ scores which context is worth keeping  
→ catches repeated actions before they burn the run  
→ gates risky tool calls and sends uncertainty to review

opus still owns the expensive part: planning, writing, coding, synthesis. jev sits around it as the decision layer.

that matters because a typical loop can have 11 decision points but only 2 real generation calls. once those are separated, latency and cost stop scaling with every tiny fork in the workflow.

AND IT'S STILL NOT TOO LATE TO START TODAY.

Nine bots. Five faceless channels. About two hours of your time a week.

And the most valuable bot in the entire setup is the one that DELETES the work.

Here’s how it runs:

Chief of Staff scores ideas and routes the work. Scout finds stories backed by primary sources. Scriptwriter turns them into 80-second scripts with seven shots. Art Director picks the look and model for each shot. Producer generates the visuals in 
@Picsart
 through MCP and checks the cost before spending credits. Editor assembles the clips, voice, music and captions. Auditor checks the last 30 published videos and rejects repetitive or unsupported work. Publisher sends cleared videos to Shorts, TikTok and Reels. Analyst reads retention and payouts every Monday and tells the team what to improve or stop doing.

42 videos made a week. Around 30 published.

Roughly $9 to produce a finished 80-second video.

No filming. No face on camera.

WHERE DOES THE MONEY COME FROM?

Four streams. Illustrative monthly numbers once you’ve built an audience:

→ Platform payouts: roughly $1,500–$2,500 at 4–5M views, depending on platform, audience and eligible views.
→ Sponsorships: two placements at $1,500 each = $3,000.
→ Your own product: a $12 download × 250 sales = $3,000 gross.
→ Memberships: 600 members × roughly $3.50 after platform cuts = $2,100.

Getting there takes an audience and testing. The setup gives you a way to do that work consistently.

Start with one channel. Finish one video. Publish it. Learn what held people’s attention. Make the next one better.

Give yourself a month of actually building something. Your first useful result could be the reason you keep going.

I put the entire setup in my article: all 9 agent prompts, the exact Picsart MCP connection steps, production costs and the monetisation breakdown.

Free. Nothing gated.

this is f*cking clever setup

64 AI agent sessions shared one memory of past decisions

the setup gave every session access to an append-only record of decisions, evidence and the reasons behind them

when an agent reaches a judgment call, it checks for a relevant recipe. that check also leaves a dated trace of what the agent was considering, so later sessions can find it

the field log: 178 recipe checks across 64 distinct agent and sub-agent sessions over 3 days

68% confirmed a prior decision and let the agent continue. about 4.5% changed the agent's action

the case that matters most: an agent decided a database index looked unused and kept its removal in an isolated commit. a human re-tested under realistic conditions, found the index was useful and reversed the change. the mistaken call, the challenge and the correction now remain in the shared record

the loop:
reach a judgment → check prior decisions → read the evidence → act within a reversible boundary → log the trace → verify the outcome → let the next agent inherit the *why*

this is one developer's self-reported field evaluation, not a benchmark or proof that 64 agents were running at once. the interesting design is the shared, inspectable decision trail

save this, then build a second brain for your product ⭣
